passage: I'm Sumit, and I was standing at the bus stop in Gangtok when the taxi slid into the parked jeep. A small bump, nobody hurt. passage:
Internship supervisor's note, 14 July

On Monday our intern Eshaan saw a delivery van reverse into a parked cycle outside the office. He came in shaken and said, 'The van just backed into it, slowly.' By Wednesday, after the videos in the office group and a post on the local news page, his version had changed: the driver was speeding, on his phone, and swore at the cyclist. When the building manager asked him to write a statement, he included all of it and said he was '100% sure'. I asked Eshaan, gently, to tell me only what he saw with his own eyes. He was quiet, then said, 'Slow reverse. That's all I saw.' I have asked him to rewrite the statement with just that, and to mark anything else as 'heard later'.

Lokesh

qa.a: 'The van just backed into it, slowly.'

qa.a: Eshaan felt confident and sure, not noticing that the new details came from videos and posts rather than his own eyes.

qa.a: It helped Eshaan separate first-hand memory from later reports, so the statement is more accurate.

qa.q: How might the van driver be affected if the first statement had been submitted?

grounding: A young adult who witnessed a minor accident adds details from later videos and news, feeling certain until asked what he saw himself.

Sarita scrolled through her phone. There it was: a photo of the whiteboard from that meeting. '38,000 incl. materials.' Both women laughed. Neither had been right. The painters were paid 38.

passage: Keerthana, you asked on the podcast how I handle fights at work. I'm Pema, and I'll tell you about the one that changed me. Last year my colleague and I argued over whether the client had asked for the blue design or the green one. I was certain: green. I could picture the client's face saying it. I raised my voice. Then someone asked, 'Did anyone write it down?' I found the meeting notes. Blue. My perfect memory was wrong. Since then, I start every disagreement with, 'This is how I remember it, but let's check.' And then I look for the email, the photo, the note. It's humbling. It also ends most fights in five minutes, because we're looking for evidence together instead of fighting each other. That's my answer to your question.

qa.a: Pema felt humbled and embarrassed, having been so certain of the green.

qa.a: The colleague probably felt frustrated at being shouted at, then relieved when the notes settled it.

passage:
Housemaster's note, St Mary's hostel, Puri, 18 October

The cyclone warning came over the radio at 4 pm: landfall expected within a day, move to the inland shelter. Most boys packed. I found Thomas in the common room, scrolling his phone, feet up. When I told him to pack, he said, 'Sir, every year they say cyclone. Nothing ever happens here.' Rehana, his classmate who is a day scholar, had come to collect her books; she said, 'My father says this one is different.' Thomas laughed. I stood beside him until he closed the phone and packed a bag, and we left on the 6 pm bus. By midnight the wind had taken the tin roof off the dining hall. I will talk with the whole house about warnings next week.

Rev. Paul, housemaster

qa.q: At what time did the warning come over the radio?
qa.a: At 4 pm.

qa.q: Why was Thomas scrolling with his feet up while others packed?
qa.a: Thomas felt relaxed and safe, sure nothing would happen because nothing bad had happened in earlier years.

qa.q: What did the housemaster do that made the difference?
qa.a: The housemaster stood beside Thomas until he packed and got him on the 6 pm bus, instead of just telling him once.

qa.a: Rehana may have felt worried and brushed off, since her father's warning was serious.

grounding: A teenager shrugs off a cyclone warning because nothing bad has happened before, until an adult makes sure he leaves.

passage:
Saturday night, Guwahati

The flood warning came on the TV at dinner: the river rising, low areas to move to higher ground. Our colony is low. Mummy started packing. I stayed on the sofa watching videos. I told Saurabh on the phone, 'Every monsoon they say flood. It never reaches us.' He said his family was leaving for his Mama's place. I rolled my eyes. It felt like any Saturday. Then Papa switched off the Wi-Fi, stood in front of me and said, 'Bag. Now.' I packed, annoyed. We drove to Mausi's in the hills at ten. At midnight Saurabh sent a photo: water up to the second step of our building. My stomach went cold. I keep thinking: I really believed it couldn't happen because it hadn't before.

Naveen

passage: The fire alarm went off at 3:15 on a Tuesday in our Hyderabad office, and I'm Usha, the one who sat through it. It was loud, but nobody stood. Sahil at the next desk glanced up, looked around the floor, and went back to his spreadsheet. The team lead kept typing. I looked at them, and they looked at each other, and all of us seemed to decide it was a drill. Ninety seconds went by. Two minutes. Then a cleaner walked quickly past with her bucket, heading for the stairs. That was it. Sahil stood, I stood, and suddenly the whole floor was moving. It was a real alarm: a small fire in the pantry, put out quickly. I still think about those two minutes. Every one of us was waiting for someone else to move first.

qa.q: What time did the fire alarm go off?
qa.a: At 3:15 on a Tuesday.

qa.q: What was Usha feeling while waiting at the desk?
qa.a: Usha felt unsure and uneasy, looking to the others for a cue and finding none.

qa.q: What could Usha do the next time an alarm goes off?
qa.a: Usha could stand up and head for the stairs straight away, since one person moving can get everyone moving.

qa.q: How might the cleaner have seen the office full of people still typing?
qa.a: The cleaner may have been surprised or worried, seeing the whole floor ignore a real alarm.

grounding: An employee sees coworkers keep working through a fire alarm, each waiting for others' cues, until one person moves.

passage:
Floor supervisor's note, call centre, Level 4

Today at 11 am the fire alarm rang. I watched from the supervisor desk. Not one agent stood. Headsets stayed on. Saurabh, on a call, looked up, saw nobody moving, and kept talking. I could see people glancing at each other, each waiting for someone else. I waited too, for about twenty seconds, which I am not proud of. Then I stood on my chair and shouted, 'Everyone out, now, stairs!' Within seconds the whole floor was up. It turned out to be burnt toast in the canteen, but that isn't the point. Next steps: I will run an unannounced drill next month, and each row will have a named person whose job is to stand first.

Tarun

qa.q: At what time did the alarm ring?
qa.a: At 11 am.

qa.q: How does Tarun feel about waiting twenty seconds?
qa.a: Tarun feels uncomfortable and not proud of it, having also been caught waiting for someone else to move.

qa.q: Why is naming a person in each row to stand first a good idea?
qa.a: Because people look to each other for cues, and one person moving breaks the frozen waiting for everyone.

qa.q: How might Saurabh have felt when Tarun shouted from the chair?
qa.a: Saurabh was probably startled and then relieved, since someone finally gave a clear signal to move.

passage:
Thursday

Fire alarm today at the bank. I was at the counter with Aditi. The siren started and the manager said, 'Probably a test.' Customers kept standing in line. Aditi looked at me. I looked at the clerk opposite, who kept counting notes. For almost three minutes nobody moved. I remember thinking, if it were real, surely someone would go. Then a security guard came running from the back, shouting to get out. Everyone left at once, bumping into each other. There was smoke from a short circuit in the server room, not big, but real. Outside, Aditi said, 'We were all waiting for each other.' She was right. I was waiting for someone to tell me what I already knew. Next time, I go first.

Joseph

qa.q: Where was the short circuit?
qa.a: In the server room.

qa.q: What was Joseph thinking during those three minutes?
qa.a: Joseph felt unsure and uneasy, thinking that if it were real someone would surely go, and waiting for a cue.

qa.q: What does Joseph decide for next time, and why does it make sense?
qa.a: To go first, because waiting for others' cues delays everyone, and one person moving helps the rest move.

qa.q: How might Aditi have seen the moment?
qa.a: Aditi noticed the whole group freezing and looking at each other, which is why she said they were all waiting.

passage:
Ankita moved into the flat next to ours in Kochi last year, and I've watched her do things I thought were a bit much. The first week, she walked the building's stairwells and noted both exits on a sticky note by her door. She keeps a small bag by the shoe rack: torch, water bottles, copies of her documents, a charger. In August, when the district sent a heavy-rain alert, she moved her scooter to higher ground and left for her sister's place that same evening. The rest of us laughed. The water only came up to the gate, and she came back two days later. I asked if she felt silly. She shrugged and said, 'A bit. I'd rather be a bit silly than late.' I don't know what she was really feeling. But last week I bought a torch.

Aadhya

qa.q: What does Ankita keep in the small bag by the shoe rack?
qa.a: A torch, water bottles, copies of her documents and a charger.

qa.q: How did Ankita seem to feel about leaving early when the water stayed at the gate?
qa.a: Ankita seemed a little embarrassed but calm and unbothered, preferring feeling silly to being late.

qa.q: Which of Ankita's habits could anyone copy?
qa.a: Noting exits, keeping a small emergency bag, and acting on official warnings without waiting for proof.

qa.q: How has Aadhya been affected by watching Ankita?
qa.a: Aadhya went from laughing at her to buying a torch, quietly starting to prepare too.

grounding: An observer describes an adult who notes exits, keeps a kit and follows warnings early, accepting the mild embarrassment of a false alarm.

passage:
Week one. Tejas moved into his first flat in Mumbai and, before unpacking, walked the stairs to find both exits. His cousin Eshaan, helping with boxes, laughed. 'Planning an escape?'

Week three. Tejas packed a small bag: torch, water, a phone charger, copies of his ID. He put it by the door. Eshaan rolled his eyes but said nothing.

Week seven. The city issued an orange alert for heavy rain at 5 pm. Tejas left the office at once and was home before the trains stopped. Eshaan, who had stayed to finish a report, spent the night on a platform. The next morning he texted Tejas: 'Okay. Exits and bag. Show me how.'

qa.q: What did Tejas put by the door in week three?
qa.a: A small bag with a torch, water, a phone charger and copies of his ID.

qa.q: How might Tejas have felt when Eshaan laughed at him in week one?
qa.a: Tejas may have felt a little embarrassed, but calm and sure it was worth doing.

qa.q: What choice in week seven made the difference?
qa.a: Leaving the office as soon as the alert came, without waiting for proof that the trains would stop.

qa.q: How does Eshaan's view change over the weeks?
qa.a: Eshaan goes from mocking to asking Tejas to show him how, after a night on the platform.

grounding: An adult notes exits, keeps a small kit and follows official warnings early, accepting mild embarrassment over being late.

passage: Gurpreet puttar, you laugh at my torch and water by the door? Sit, let your Siddharth Taya tell you why. In 1998 I was a young man of twenty-five, working in the mill office in Ludhiana. There was an earthquake warning on the radio. Most people shrugged. I went home early and moved my parents out of the old brick room into the courtyard for the night. The neighbours laughed; my friend Harpal called me 'Earthquake Singh' for months. Nothing happened that night. I felt foolish, I won't lie. But two years later, when the floods came, I was the one who left early, and I had a bag ready. Harpal's family lost their papers. So yes, puttar, I'll take a little laughing over being late.

qa.q: In which year did the earthquake warning come?
How did Siddharth feel when nothing happened that night?
qa.a: Siddharth felt foolish and embarrassed, especially with Harpal's teasing.

qa.q: Which choice inside the story mattered most, and why?
qa.a: Leaving early with a ready bag when the floods came, because acting on warnings kept his family's papers safe while Harpal's were lost.

qa.q: How might Harpal's family have felt after the floods?
qa.a: Harpal's family probably felt shaken and regretful, having lost their papers by not acting early.

grounding: An elder explains why he follows warnings early and keeps a kit, preferring the embarrassment of a false alarm to being late.

passage: On the first hot day of summer term at the Bhopal school, the canteen line buzzed with the same news: if you swallow a watermelon seed, a watermelon grows inside you. Lalit heard it from Binita in the morning. At recess three more children said it. By lunch, a boy in 6C swore his cousin had needed an operation. Lalit had laughed at breakfast. By the last bell, he was carefully spitting every seed out of his watermelon slice onto a napkin, and he felt a small wobble in his tummy whenever he thought about the one he'd swallowed last week. When the science teacher heard, she smiled and said, 'Seeds don't grow in stomachs.' Lalit nodded, but he still spat out the seeds.

qa.q: What did the children say happens if you swallow a watermelon seed?
qa.a: A watermelon grows inside you.

qa.q: How did Lalit feel thinking about the seed he swallowed last week?
qa.a: Lalit felt worried, with a small wobble in his tummy, because the story had started to feel true after hearing it so often.

qa.q: What could Lalit ask himself the next time a 'fact' spreads?
qa.a: Where it came from and who actually knows, instead of believing it because many people repeat it.

qa.q: How might the science teacher see the children's worry?
qa.a: The teacher finds it amusing but also sees how quickly a repeated story can feel true to children.

grounding: A child believes a 'fact' because everyone repeats it; hearing it often makes it feel familiar and true.

passage:
Monday, the first day of the Christmas holidays. At the colony gate, Zubin told Hansa, 'If you whistle at night, ghosts come.' Hansa laughed. 'That's silly.'

Wednesday. Hansa heard it again from the twins upstairs and from the vegetable seller's son. Everyone said it the same way. She didn't laugh this time.

Friday night. Walking back from the carol singing, Hansa's little brother started whistling. Hansa grabbed his arm. 'Stop! Ghosts!' He stared at her. 'Who said?' She opened her mouth. 'Everyone.' 'But who saw a ghost?' Hansa couldn't answer. She still made him stop whistling.

qa.q: What did Zubin say happens if you whistle at night?
qa.a: Ghosts come.

qa.q: Why did Hansa grab her brother's arm on Friday night?
qa.a: Hansa felt scared, because hearing the saying from so many people had made it feel true.

qa.q: What question could help Hansa think it through?
qa.a: Her brother's question, 'But who saw a ghost?', helps her notice that repetition is not the same as proof.

qa.q: How might Hansa's brother see her sudden fear?
qa.a: Her brother is puzzled, since he has not heard the saying so often and just wants to know who saw a ghost.

grounding: Over a week, a child comes to believe a ghost 'fact' because everyone repeats it, so it feels familiar and true.

passage: Gurleen beti, you won't sit under the tamarind tree because 'everyone says' a ghost lives there? Let me, your Zeenat Nani, tell you a story. The Eid I was nine, in Lucknow, all my cousins said that if you ate a sweet before namaz, you'd get worms. My older cousin said it. The girls next door said it. Even the halwai's son said it. I didn't believe it at first. By the third time I heard it, I was sure. That whole Eid morning I didn't touch a single sevaiyan until after namaz, and I was so hungry I cried. My Abbu laughed and asked who had got worms from sevaiyan. I couldn't name one person. Only that everyone said so. That's when I learned, beti: hearing something many times makes it feel true, but it doesn't make it true.

qa.q: What did Zeenat's cousins say would happen if you ate a sweet before namaz?
qa.a: You'd get worms.

qa.q: How did Zeenat feel that Eid morning?
qa.a: Zeenat felt so hungry and worried that she cried, because the repeated claim had come to feel true.

qa.q: What question inside the story changed Zeenat's mind?
qa.a: Abbu asking who had actually got worms from sevaiyan, which showed nobody could name a single case.

qa.q: How might Abbu have seen young Zeenat's refusal?
qa.a: Abbu found it funny and a little sweet, and used a gentle question to help her think.

grounding: An elder recalls believing a food 'fact' because everyone repeated it, until asked for a single real example.
